analysis.one_liner: Connects Texas's isolated power grid to neighboring grids and subject it to federal oversight.
analysis.headline: A bill to link Texas's power grid to its neighbors, with 15 Democratic cosponsors, sits untouched in the House Energy and Commerce Committee after referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Texas runs its own power grid, ERCOT, deliberately cut off from neighboring grids so federal regulators have no say over it. This bill ends that isolation. It would force ERCOT to build transmission connections to nearby grids large enough to import or export power, and it would bring ERCOT under the authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission like every other grid in the country. The connections would have to be finished by 2037, with priorities for renewable energy, cheaper siting, community input, and union apprenticeship jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Texas households and businesses gain a backstop against the grid failures that caused hundreds of deaths during the 2021 winter blackout, because they could import power from neighboring states when ERCOT's own supply falls short. Renewable energy producers gain access to much larger markets, and construction workers gain projects with prevailing-wage and apprenticeship requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Texas households and renewable energy producers

how_it_helps.text: Requires minimum transfer capability between ERCOT and neighboring grids — 4.3 to 12.6 gigawatts to SPP, 2.5 to 16.2 to MISO, and 2.6 to 7.9 to the Western Interconnection — to be completed by January 1, 2037 [S2].
Repeals the Federal Power Act exemptions that have kept ERCOT outside federal regulators' jurisdiction since the 1930s, subjecting it to the same rules as every other US grid [S2].
Tripling of federal transmission financing: raises the Transmission Facilitation Program's borrowing authority from $2.5 billion to $13.5 billion to help pay for the new lines [S2].

Siting plans must prioritize grid-enhancing technologies, existing highway and railroad rights-of-way, degraded land, renewable access, community involvement for environmental-justice and Tribal communities, and registered apprenticeships with prevailing wages [S2].
Requires a Department of Energy study of the reliability and cost benefits of linking the Texas grid to Mexico's [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The cost of building the transmission lines falls on electricity customers — Texas ratepayers and those in neighboring grids — plus the $11 billion increase in federal borrowing authority, which is taxpayer-backed. Texas power generators also give up scarcity profits they currently earn when local shortages spike prices.

drawbacks.text: Building thousands of miles of transmission lines is expensive, and the bill does not say who allocates the costs; ratepayers in Texas and neighboring grids would bear them [S2].

The bill repeals ERCOT's Federal Power Act exemptions, so Texas loses its autonomy from federal regulators and from shared-cost arrangements with other regions — a trade-off ERCOT's structure was designed to avoid [S2].

Interconnection can raise Texas electricity prices in normal times, because ERCOT's isolation today keeps its power among the cheapest in the country while giving up the scarcity-price spikes that made it dangerous in emergencies.
New lines remain subject to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act reviews, which can slow construction on the same timeline the bill mandates [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reliability benefit is real and large — an isolated grid that failed catastrophically in 2021 gains the ability to import emergency power — but the bill is honest that this is not free: it trades some of Texas's cheap, unregulated-grid independence for security, at a cost of billions in transmission construction, largely paid by ratepayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on February 26, 2026, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Greg Casar of Texas introduced the Connect the Grid Act on February 26, 2026 [S1].

Fourteen other House members joined as original cosponsors, including Ocasio-Cortez, Escobar, Garcia of Texas, Green of Texas, Doggett, Crockett, Castro of Texas, Espaillat, Garcia of California, Frost, Tlaib, Jayapal, and Ramirez [S2].
All 15 cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support [S3].
The bill's only action since introduction was referral to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; no further action appears in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: ERCOT and the Texas power industry are better off so far: the grid remains isolated and outside federal regulators' authority, preserving the current arrangement. Transmission developers and workers lose the construction projects the bill would have funded.

for.name: Rep. Greg Casar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Connect the Grid Act to interconnect ERCOT with neighboring grids and end its federal exemptions.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), Escobar (D-TX), Doggett (D-TX), Crockett (D-TX), Jayapal (D-WA)

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee has taken no action since referral [S3, S4].

industries.note: ERCOT's isolation lets Texas generators charge extreme prices during local shortages and operate outside federal oversight. Interconnection lets cheaper power flow in during emergencies, cutting those windfalls and ending the exemption that protects them.
The bill repeals the Federal Power Act provisions that let ERCOT avoid FERC jurisdiction and cost-sharing with other regions. Its independent-gatekeeper status over the Texas grid would end.

The bill mandates new transmission facilities by 2037 and triples the federal Transmission Facilitation Program's borrowing authority to $13.5 billion, with prevailing-wage and apprenticeship requirements for the construction workforce.
Siting plans must prioritize transmission that expands access to wind, solar, and geothermal power, giving renewables in Texas and neighboring regions access to much larger markets.

analysis.trajectory: A Democrat-only bill in a House with Republican control of the Energy and Commerce Committee has little path to a floor vote. Barring a change in committee leadership's priorities or a shift in control, it is likely to sit in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 and expire without action.
